transcript:
# COMMITTEE ON JOINT SCHOOL BUILDINGS
March 10, 2026 at 5:00 PM

Chairman O'Connell called the meeting to order.

The Clerk called the roll.

Present: Aldermen Bonilla, Fajardo (arrived 5:09PM)
School Committee Members O'Connell, Turner, Hamer

Absent: Alderman Thomas

Messrs.: Alderman Sapienza, M. Upton, J. Soucy, M. Lenfest, H. Cobanoglu

Chairman O'Connell: Before we get to the first item on the agenda tonight, we're going to see if we have an opportunity for people to address the board. I don't have the formal writing here, but I've spoken to Alderman Sapienza prior to the meeting, and he has a question and a comment. So, we'll hear from Alderman Sapienza.

Alderman Sapienza: Thanks for the opportunity. So could someone hopefully explain to me how it is that in December of 2023, the Board of School Committee approved a $290 million bond for phase one, and now I'm finding out that $62.6 million has been spent in cash so far for phase one. I'll read it off here really quick: because project spending has progressed more slowly than originally projected, the school district has been able to fund approximately $62.6 million of the $306 million project cost with cash. Now, that might sound like fiscal responsibility, but I mean, the analogy was made at the last aldermen meeting that it's kind of like making a higher down payment on a house to keep the payments lower for the next 30 years. That sounds good, but you don't do that if you're broke, which we are. We're staring into the face of a very sizable deficit. I mean, $62.6 million is approximately a quarter of the overall school budget for fiscal year 2027, approximately. That's a lot of money to spend in cash when you actually don't have a lot of money. If somebody can help me make that make sense, that would be great.

Chairman O'Connell: I don't think we've got the right people in the room to answer that because this is an issue for finance. We do have LeftField in the room, who is responsible. So, we can answer part of that, but not the question you actually asked. They can tell you what monies have been spent to the last penny, but with regard to the sources of the funding, bonding, anticipatory notes, and financials, that's not the purview of LeftField. They're managing the project and every dollar that's spent within it. So, they can answer those questions. So, we could start with, for instance, the number you quote, the $62 million that's been spent in cash.

Alderman Sapienza: LeftField seems like some terrific folks. They're like an objective third party. Who greenlighted $62.6 million cash, when in fact we had a $290 million bond greenlighted?

Chairman O'Connell: Having said, first of all, that the people involved in the decision, I'm not certain of the $62 million number, but if that is the right number, I don't know what it is. It changes regularly. The people who have been responsible for it and have been managing that are the financial people at the school district, which is Karen DeFrancis and then on the city side, our city finance director, Sharon Wickens, as well as bonding council and some other entities whose titles I've forgotten, who are at the level of advisors on bonds. I can add something else, which is at the outset of this project, the estimated cost of financing $290 million of bonding was $17 million per year. So, I just want to be clear, I don't have the numbers written in front of me, so I'm giving you the best I can to help us all to move forward, now it is around $17.7 million. As the years proceed, it's anticipated that if we were to bond the full $290 million, that $17 million would be needed year over year over year out over time. And so one of the factors is you don't want to get into a point where you don't use the $17 million for the purpose that you might be alluding to. For instance, take the $17 million and pay salaries and ongoing expenses for general expenses. What that would do is the year that the bonding was done, first of all, the bond would be a full $290 million, and the year at which you issued the bonds, you would have to find $17 million in the budget. And now the taxpayers would have a hole of $17 million that would need to be filled on unanticipated or at least anticipated, because everybody knew about it. But the money's not in the budget. And the school district would be going to the Board of Mayor and Aldermen saying we're in year three of this project. We're issuing the final bonds. The full note now needs to be paid annually, and it's $17 million a year. And oh, by the way, we didn't have the $17 million in the budget for the last three years. So now we want you to give it to us. So, the $17 million was put aside. The $17 million has been used to pay down, as you call it, cash. So, it's been used to pay down the anticipated costs. So now I don't know what the latest number is, but for instance, the modular work was paid for out of that $17 million. And so, it's gone for that purpose because that budget item needs to be maintained so that there is not a shock to the taxpayers in year three. The premise on which this project was approved by the Board of Mayor and Aldermen was that this project would not affect or increase the tax cap compliant number in the City of Manchester. It was being done within the existing budget and that was the case, and the anticipation was that the school district would continue to get funded at the cost-of-living increase over time. What was not anticipated was that the Board of Mayor and Aldermen would pass budgets that would reduce our funding. For instance, in the last two years, it has reduced our funding $17 million below the cost-of-living increase, which has caused us to have a $16 million hole this year. So, we didn't have a hole before the hole was made. Another point I'd like to make is that the Board of Mayor and Aldermen last year passed a budget in the City of Manchester, which reduced taxes for the families and taxpayers of Manchester for the schools by 2.4%, creating a bigger hole. And that was made up by that money; the $17 million isn't a separate bucket. The $17 million is part of the money that the school district has. Last year we had to spend $10 million in emergency funds because of the reasons I just outlined. What has been happening is that now we anticipate that the eventual cost of this project, which will come in under budget and on time, we're confident of that, but that the anticipated loan will not be as high as $290 million. Whatever the new number is, I don't want to risk saying it here today because I don't know what it is, but I do know that the annual cost of the loan will go down to $16 million or below. So, that is an oversight of where we are. The last thing I will say, and I'll let you respond, is that all of this is being done by the best advice we can get from bonding counsel out of New York, Boston, our own finance director and finance department, and Karen DeFrancis, and is seen by all of those people who advise us as fiscally responsible and as the prudent thing to do and the right thing to do by the taxpayers of Manchester.

Matt Upton, Executive Director of Legal & Policy of the Manchester School District: When the original bond was approved, the spending authority was $306 million. The amount of bonding authority was $290 million at the time that that was approved. There was a representation made by both the Board of School Committee and the BMA that it would have no impact on the tax rate. What the chairman has said is, in fact, correct. If we started spending that $17 million on operating costs, that money would not exist when the bond had to be issued. Now, if we had issued the bond back at the time, we had gotten the authority and we didn't need it at the time. We could utilize bond anticipation notes which is what we've been doing here at a much lower interest rate, so that the overall cost of the project has been reduced. But let's say we did bond the $290 million back when the spending authority was given. That $17 million would be gone. We'd be paying on it right now and there would be no $17 million available. We're talking about the possibility this year of using some portion of that to actually offset some of the costs of the budget. This is the smartest thing we can do. And you can talk to Sharon Wickens. There are a number of people who are very independent in this who will tell you this is what we were advised to do and made the most sense.

Alderman Sapienza: I'll just briefly conclude with this. This can get rather complex. I'm not claiming to be a municipal bond expert, but when I see that the school spent $62.6 million cash and we're looking at a $16 million deficit this coming fiscal year minimum, it doesn't add up. Yes, it can get complex, but you can also simplify it. $62.6 million cash. To me, it doesn't add up. I'm going to say thank you and goodbye and let these folks make their presentation. Obviously, this is going to come up again as we enter the budget discussions.

Chairman O'Connell: I appreciate your interest in being here. You know, there are 28 public representatives, 29, including the mayor in the city of Manchester. It's not lost on me that you're here and making your point and seeking clarity. So, I appreciate that. I want to encourage you and others to come. This is the place to be doing this. You know, there may be other venues, but it's certainly appropriate here. So, I just would say to you, the $62 million seems to me that that includes bond and treasury notes because the Manchester School District can only have used $17 million, that is the most money that's there. So, if that was a full three years, it's $51 million. So, if you use the entire $17 million per year for the full three years, it'll be $51 million. I do know that a bond anticipatory note for $28 million has already been drawn down. I know that there's a further bond anticipatory note that will be drawn down in financial year 2026-27. That bond, if you really want to get into details of it, will pay off the first anticipatory bond and it will pay off, then it will add more, and that's done for the purposes of minimizing the cost of doing this project. I disagree with you with great respect. First of all, you said the word cash like you emphasized it.

Alderman Sapienza: I'm reading it off this document.

Chairman O'Connell: What's the document?

Alderman Sapienza: This is the document that Sharon Wickens was nice enough to send out; I didn't make this document up. She put it together.

Chairman O'Connell: So again, Sharon isn't here to speak for herself. I'm sure she'll speak as appropriate and anytime she's asked to at the Chambers. But she has been integral to this process and I'm sure I haven't seen what you've got, but I'm certain because I know from speaking to her that she would not say anything that would say, I don't agree or I don't think this is right or I think this is wrong. So, whatever she gave you, she gave you the answer to the question. Not knowing what you're looking at, I can say with great certainty she did not say I think we could have done it another way or this wasn't wise, because that's not what she and all the other experts are saying. We have a disagreement here; you're disagreeing with the best advice the city can get from the best people we can find on the east coast. They are unanimous in saying that this is the right way to do it. I understand your point, but at some point, you also have to recognize that the voices who do know about it and are trained in the subject and are paid to look after the best interests of the taxpayers, are telling you very clearly this is the right way to do this, and this is the best value for the people of Manchester.

Alderman Sapienza: We're supposed to just leave it to the experts? I'm looking at again, $62.6 million cash. I'm not making that up. I'll send you this email here. I admit I'm not a municipal bond expert. I know there are experts out there, but if we're looking at a deficit of $16 million at a bare minimum for the school budget, and I'm reading on this document that Sharon Wickens was nice enough to prepare, and it says that this $62.6 million cash has been spent, I have to ask some questions. It doesn't add up to me.

Chairman O'Connell: With great respect, it doesn't add up to you, but it adds up to everybody else in the room.

Alderman Sapienza: It does?

Alderman Bonilla: I definitely would further ask Sharon about the $62 million cash. Ask her to break it down. All of us are meeting together soon in the next couple of weeks. I would save that question there so you could ask them to really break it down. You've mentioned the question about three times, and I hear you. So just mention it there. We'll have all the experts.

Alderman Sapienza: Everybody should have the document that I have. It's public. It's not confidential.

Alderman Bonilla: If you don't mind sharing it with everybody.

Alderman Sapienza: Sure.

1. Presentation from LeftField regarding the School District Priority One Project to date.

Jennifer Soucy, Project Manager at SMMA: We thought with the new board coming aboard this year, it would be appropriate to do a design update for the board to share where we're at with the designs, where we're at with the project, and open it up if there's any questions. So, with that, I do have a lot of slides because we do have a lot of good things to share.

Chairman O'Connell: Just so my colleagues on the board know, the purpose of this is especially to for members Hamer and Fajardo and Bonilla, to all of us really, but especially for you, to bring everybody up to speed.

J. Soucy: We'll start with the middle schools; Hillside Middle School, up on the screen is the proposed site plan. So, you see the existing building, Reservoir Ave is on your left. And then the new addition, which if you've driven by there, you can actually see it pretty prominently from the road. It's on the back side, the north side of the building. It's roughly 42,000ft². So, this school, once complete, will accommodate 1,200 students. Some other site improvements that we're doing is adding a parking lot for staff. The parking lot that exists there now where all the construction trailers are, that will be removed and the city has a plan to restore that to an athletic field after the end of the project. We are creating a loop road around the building and where the temporary modular classroom building is now that will be removed and that will become play space just outside of the existing cafeteria. So just sharing a couple renderings; this is a couple views of the new main entrance. We're constructing a new canopy at the main entrance, new signage, all new windows. On the upper image you can see the three-story addition peeking up in the background. This is a view of the new addition. Again, I said three stories. The first floor of the addition is actually the new media center. So, one thing that we've tried to incorporate in all of the new middle school designs is to make the media center more accessible. Right now, they're sort of buried on the second floor within the buildings. So, there's direct access from the exterior. So, it really will become a community resource after hours. It will be easily accessible, lots of nice large windows, natural light. On the left, you can see the existing cafeteria. We will be replacing windows, making them larger. Adding some more light into those spaces. This is a view of the main entry lobby with all of the middle schools. We also are trying to make the entrances more welcoming. So, we've incorporated some graphic walls. And just conceptually we're trying to draw inspiration from local landscapes, industries, different local inspiration. So, this design is actually reminiscent of the Amoskeag Falls and it's just conceptual, but it's to honor that. We're also incorporating some specialty ceilings, which are wood look ceilings. So, it'll give that space a lot of warmth as you enter into the space. This is a view of the new media center. So, you could see the windows to the exterior in the back. Also, incorporating some of this wood look ceiling to add some warmth into the space. We're adding a lot of flexible furniture, a lot of different zones in that space. Another view just looking in the other direction, you can see again, a lot of the different furniture areas that we're creating. And we'll have a makerspace in a separate classroom that'll be open just off of the library. This is a view of one of the new spaces in the addition. This is an art classroom on the upper level of the addition. So, with the higher ceilings and exposed structure, it's a more industrial looking type space. I'll go through McLaughlin and then I'm happy to take any questions on any of the projects. So, McLaughlin, you could see the "U" shape of the existing building. The addition is actually finishing that loop and tying in or linking the two public spaces, the gym on the right, and then the cafeteria on the left. Largely the site's circulation remains the same. We are going to be making this section in front of the building two way to help improve some of the circulation because right now you have to loop around the entire building. So, some minor improvements to the site. Also, when we link these with the new additions, we're creating an exterior courtyard space, which is a nice secure space where we'll have outdoor learning classroom space. Also creating some outdoor play area on the backside of the building for the new fifth grade. This is a view of the new addition. So, this is the new main entrance to the building or relocating all of the admin spaces up to the new addition. And then on the second floor will be the media center which will be easily accessible to the public as well after hours. So, you can see that prominently displayed opening up to the community. This is a view of the backside of the addition. So, this is that interior courtyard with some outdoor classroom spaces, lots of nice windows and natural light. This is a view of the main entry lobby. You can see the two-story open stair which will lead you up to the media center. A lot of the graphic design in here draws inspiration from the fall in New Hampshire and all the bright colors of the landscape. Just the second floor of that addition. And this is the entrance to the media center. Lots of open glazing. And this is a view inside the media center. This is the circulation desk. Lots of color, lots of flexible furniture, and then a view. Also, within the addition, we have a new makerspace lab type space. So again, open ceilings. Southside is very similar to Hillside. This will accommodate 1,200 students. So, because Southside, Parkside and Hillside are almost identical buildings, our approach to the addition and location are very similar. So, you can see that's on the north side of the building. As far as site improvements, we are trying to make some improvements with adding some layover drop off area in front of the building and accessible parking close to the main entrance. So, you can see that's where the number one and number five and six are in this diagram site. The rest of the circulation around the site will largely remain as it exists right now. We are going to create a hardscape area play area in the front of the building along South Jewett Street, which will have basketball courts. So, we're relocating those from the back of the building into the front.

Chairman O'Connell: For future board members who will be here in the future, if you look to the top end of that, where the parking lot is above the number for that parking lot right there. So, it was hoped in this project, it was never part of the project, it didn't make it into the cut. So, it's not as though we reduced the scope. But as part of the long-term planning, there are a couple of things for the fields and areas for these schools. There's a hope that that area that's now scrubland or whatever, that area right there that had we gone the full hog, so to speak, we would have put a playing field right there. It's set up for it. It's the right place to do it. There is also the field next to Hillside, which is in the CIP budget for a future date that would have a field there.

Alderman Fajardo: Are you referring to the football field or that small parking area?

Chairman O'Connell: I'm referring to the area right there where she's circulating with the cursor. So, it would be the hope that when funding is available, there's not actually a plan, as such that exists for that right now, it's certainly not part of this, for your information, as we go forward, this is what the right thing to do for these schools would be. Our middle schools need playing fields.

J. Soucy: There's an opportunity there for future development.

Chairman O'Connell: And the parking lot is there now and the access to the parking lot is there. So, it's kind of easy.

J. Soucy: So, this is a view of the new addition, more street facing on this side. So, we've also tried to incorporate school colors in some of the exterior elements, but also all throughout the interior of the building. Again, the media center located on the first floor with lots of glazing. And then this is a view of the main entrance lobby. So, this is taking inspiration from the White Mountains and the landscape of the mountains. This is a view of the media center here at Southside. Again, they all have similar elements, although they are unique in their own designs, but we are trying to create some consistency and parity between all the middle schools. Just another view again, of the circulation desk and the different furniture zones in the makerspace that's off of this library as well. So, Parkside, this school is designed for 800 students. So, the addition is on the back side, the north side of the building, a two-story addition in this case so a little bit smaller. From a site perspective, we are making some improvements with drop off along the main entrance, but also around the back of the building again, keeping in place the playground area for the most part, as we know that this was recently improved. There's a futsal court, some basketball courts that will be relocated and incorporated into the final design. And then we are creating a loop road, formalizing that for emergency access around the building. This is a view of the addition. Again, the media center on the first floor. And then the view of the main entrance lobby, which takes its inspiration from the textile industry, the Amoskeag textiles that are local. And a view of the entrance to the media center, again, you could see some of the floor design incorporating that design concept in the media center here at Parkside. And then a view of the art space up in the new addition as well.

Chairman O'Connell: You've been alluding to the textiles, the White Mountains, and other stuff. For those who are interested in the artistry or conceptual nature of what was done here, a lot of thought went into all of that, both the design, the colors, and they're tied into various things from the Amoskeag Falls to different elements and the schools each have their own and the whole color palette comes from that. I mean, it's work you guys do every day so you're not as impressed with it as someone like me who doesn't realize the amount of creative and artistic effort that goes into this. A lot of thought from our team goes into it and a lot of planning. The number that struck me just as we looked at that, I think it's worth noting there are a lot of indirect benefits that are happening here. For instance, the road around Parkside; right now, there's no road around Parkside. If you ask the police or the fire department, the fire department is thrilled that they now have access to that school instead of driving in mud if there was a problem there, God forbid. That's a consequence. These are big improvements, small, but big improvements. One of the key things, if you're looking at these buildings, is if you go to those middle schools today, they have steps and there's a ramp to one side. Those are all being eliminated; the ground is going to be raised so the whole area outside will be leveled with the front doors. So, there won't be need for special ramps for people who are not ambulatory or disabled or whatever. People have ease of access, and those kinds of things are repeated around the building. So besides what we see here in terms of these wonderful spaces that are going to be great for students to learn in, there are lots of other incremental differences.

School Committee Member Hamer: A quick comment on the Parkside steps. I was there recently. I hadn't been there in a year or two, and it seems like the steps got steeper because everything is sinking. I had somebody with me that I that I had to help up the steps because they've gotten bigger. I think that's a great point. That road around there, I mean, it's a disaster the way it is now with Gossler Park right next to it and when it comes time to do drop off and pick-ups and things like that. That's a great improvement. I think people will recognize that for sure.

Alderman Fajardo: I just wanted to ask, in terms of the imagery that you were sharing, the renderings, to what extent are these conceptual, to what extent are they considered final?

J. Soucy: I would say they're very late in the design process, so there may be little tweaks, but for the most part, conceptually that's what the design is currently.

Alderman Fajardo: When we walk in someday it should look familiar to those of us who saw these slides.

Chairman O'Connell: And now the moment I know that, at very minimum, Alderman Bonilla has been waiting for, Beech Street School.

J. Soucy: The site plan for the new Beech is across the street from the current Beech Street School. So, it's at the current Sheridan-Emmet Park site. The configuration of the new school is sited this way primarily because we have an underground culvert, historically there's a historic brook that runs pretty much right directly through the middle of the site basically following the profile of the building. So, we didn't want to build on the culvert, but we also kind of took inspiration from that. And, conceptually, we've called it the edge of the brook. Similar to how a lot of the mill buildings follow the rivers as well through the city. So, Beech Street is on your right. We've created from a site perspective, a loading area, a bus or parent drop off area on the site itself. The site is really tight and it's complex in terms of its geometry, but we were able to create a drop off area with some limited parking because a lot of the parking for staff will be across the way. We are going to be doing some improvements along Beech Street for crossing and working with city traffic on those elements that we're going to be adding to the street.

Alderman Fajardo: I was actually wondering about traffic. And you just mentioned that you're working with our highway department.

J. Soucy: We are.

Alderman Fajardo: Is there any anticipation on your part of when this street will ultimately be going from two lanes down to one? Is that something that you're considering?

J. Soucy: We're not. Currently, we're not considering going down to one lane. It's still two lanes.

Alderman Fajardo: I am considering that almost every day.

J. Soucy: We do have improvements. We are going to be adjusting some of the curb lines that are sort of traffic calming measures that we've been working with city traffic on. That will help.

Chairman O'Connell: There will be paperwork going before the Committee on Public Safety, Health & Traffic. That will be coming forward pretty soon to do the crosswalk here on the bottom right-hand corner. And you'll see there's a bump out right there. So that actually has a kind of a traffic-calming effect. There is a layby where it says bus loading there. So that's actually so shorter buses, etc. will be able to pull in there and there is going to be a lane to the right. Today, that's a sidewalk and parking, but now it's going to be a layby area. This will be an enhanced crosswalk crossing Beech Street. When the work is done on the right-hand side, on the east side of this thing where the current Beech Street School is, where there will be a field, a soccer field, etc., there'll be fencing to stop balls coming onto the street and all that. But another effect it will have is that people will not be able to or inclined to cross across the street at those points. The fencing will bring them down to the point where that crosswalk is. For those of you in ward five, there is a footpath that goes easterly from about where the crosswalk is along the side of that field. So, it connects over onto Maple Street. And that's a tree lined footpath that is envisioned under the later phases of this project. I love the single lane Beech and Maple and others north of Bridge. I think it would be great if they were able to be done, that would be an enhancement to this. But for now, the traffic calming piece or maybe it's not being sold as that, but the bump outs will serve that purpose. And there is also going to be something coming before your board as well with regard to a crosswalk not shown here, but on the western side crossing Union as well. So, and also the work to change Green Street to one way will be part of that package. It's a minor change, but you'll be seeing that in the coming months.

Alderman Bonilla: So, with the bump out right there on Beech Street, do we get the little yellow flashing lights?

J. Soucy: Yes, the rectangular rapid flashing lights.

Alderman Bonilla: And then on the Union side, do we get a bump out there as well?

J. Soucy: This site plan doesn't reflect it. That was a more recent request from traffic, but yes.

Alderman Bonilla: Do we get the yellow flashing lights?

J. Soucy: Not on Union Street.

Hamdi Cobanoglu, Senior Project Manager at LeftField: Just a crosswalk.

J. Soucy: The city could do that project as well.

Alderman Bonilla: We'll take it up with them after.

Chairman O'Connell: That's been sort of, and we're not complaining about it, but it's been a sort of an add because it we didn't make it part of this project originally, it wasn't envisioned that that crosswalk or something would happen on Union Street. Not just on the Beech Street project, but on all four projects, fire, police, traffic, engineering, DPW have all been involved. And if I could take this moment to say that the work, the people in our city departments and the cooperation that has existed on this project, there have been many meetings for many different things. And the internal security of buildings, student safety, traffic, and environmental impacts, everybody at the state level and others. But at the city, I want to call out the city departments, especially DPW, for the amount of cooperation over the last two years that they've been doing. I think everybody on the project would say that it's been a pleasure to work with them. And we've heard it again and again, not because I'm from Manchester, but we've heard it again and again from the teams of architects and engineers who are in the city working on this, that they have lots of good things to say about our staff.

Alderman Fajardo: I'm not surprised to hear that at all. I think we are very fortunate to have a ton of really intelligent experts right here within our city staff.

J. Soucy: I certainly would agree with that. It's been very collaborative and very productive. So, continuing on just to finish out on the site, just south of the building is a new playground area. So, they'll have play structures as well as a full basketball court and hardscape area. Also, on the north of the building, there's a smaller play space, more intimate, just outdoor classroom space. And that's just off of the kindergarten wing. So, kindergarten and first grade will be on the first floor. The gym and the cafeteria, which we anticipate fully being heavily used by the community, are off of Beech Street on the eastern portion of the site facing Beech Street. We have some images coming up of those spaces as well. This is just an aerial view. So, Beech Street on your right, just showing the site and how the massing of the building shapes up. I do want to point out, the main entrance is right in the center here where there's a canopy. And then above that you can see this little carve out where we'll be creating a roof terrace. So, it's a nice exterior enclosed safe space for kids to have outdoor learning, but also, it's right off of the media center. So, it can become a nice community use space after hours as well.

Chairman O'Connell: When you enter that main entrance, you take a right, you've got the cafeteria and then the gym all off your right for community use purposes. And it's a very large space, but on your left on the ground floor on your left is community rooms. There are a bunch of, if you were to take a left, there's a bunch of rooms there for community purposes to the left. And it's designed again to be used out of school hours so that there are bathrooms available, etc., and the rest of the school can be closed off.

Alderman Fajardo: This is intended to exist as a community center?

Chairman O'Connell: A community school.

Alderman Fajardo: Is that true?

J. Soucy: Correct. There'll be spaces that will serve that community school function.

Chairman O'Connell: The community school designation is a designation and we've been able to do things under that designation, but I think more broadly, all our schools as a school district, we're moving to a place with all of these schools where we're anticipating that they'll be used by the community. headline: Accepted February 2026 status and financial report on school building projects; discussed $62.6 million cash spending and construction schedules.
summary: An alderman questioned why $62.6 million had been spent in cash on the Priority One school building project despite an approved $290 million bond, and city officials explained the funding approach. LeftField and SMMA presented design updates for Hillside, McLaughlin, Southside, Parkside, and Beech Street schools, along with construction schedules through 2028. The committee voted to accept the February 2026 monthly status and financial report from LeftField and submit it to the Board of Mayor and Aldermen and Board of School Committee for informational purposes.
decisions: Voted to accept the February 2026 monthly status and financial report from LeftField and submit it to the Board of Mayor and Aldermen and Board of School Committee for informational purposes (Alderman Thomas and School Committee Member Turner absent).
